# Detecting Feature-Level Target Leakage with Language Models: A Source-Grounded Benchmark

*Draft v2. Every number in this manuscript is regenerated by `verify_paper.py`
and appears in `NUMBERS.txt`. Nothing is quoted from memory. Section references
of the form [N §k] point to that file.*

---

## Abstract

A feature leaks when its value encodes the outcome it is used to predict. This
is distinct from the other failures called "leakage" — duplicated units across
a split, train/test contamination, identifier columns — and it cannot be fixed
by any splitting scheme, because the column is wrong in every split.

We build a benchmark for it: **15 datasets, 604 columns, 68 documented
positives** — **12 datasets and 40 positives** coded from documentation, and a
held-out **3 datasets and 28 positives** whose sources name the leaking column
themselves — plus a third stratum of external validation and a fourth of
mechanically verified positives. The two main strata were admitted under
different rules and are never pooled in any result; the combined figure is given
here once, for scale. Each positive
is licensed by a written record, most by a verbatim quotation from the
dataset's own documentation, and every coded derivation implying a testable
pattern in the values is checked against them — one source statement is refuted
by its own data and withdrawn.

On this benchmark the best model reading only column names and a target reaches
**F1 0.905**, and the best figure anywhere on the condition ladder is **0.929**
— against **0.630** for a correlation baseline whose threshold was swept on the
answers, and **0.394** for a keyword rule over column names whose vocabulary was
fitted the same way. The gain from adding a derivation criterion is concentrated in the
models that were failing without it: resampling datasets, every interval that
excludes zero belongs to a model scoring under 0.66 without it, and the three
strongest models are all consistent with no effect (§6.5). On a held-out set whose labels are named by their sources,
one model is **exact at the primary condition** — 84 true positives, zero false
positives, zero false negatives across 894 column judgments, though those are
298 columns judged three times with an identical answer each time rather than
894 independent ones (§9). Cleaning a dataset
with a model's flags lands **0.024 F1** from the ceiling a documented cleaning
achieves; the correlation baseline lands **0.048** away and errs in both
directions, keeping a leak on one dataset and deleting the most useful
legitimate feature on another. The leakage is worth finding: leaving the
documented columns in inflates F1 by **0.147** on average and 0.306 at worst.

We then ask whether any of this is an artefact of where we looked. Sweeping
**8,693 Kaggle datasets, 605 competitions, 14,420 Hugging Face cards and 6,418
OpenML records** — four documentation cultures, none of them the archive the
instruments were written on — the sieve fires at a comparable rate everywhere
and yields **two** admissible records in total. One of them, a 2026 chess table
that postdates most of the roster's training data, carries the largest
downstream effect in the paper (**ΔF1 0.632**); the other is documented as
leakage by its own uploader and costs **−0.003** to remove. Scarcity of
*documented* leakage replicates in every population we can reach, and detection
survives on tables this project did not choose.

The failures are more informative than the successes. Models operationalise
leakage as *timing*. Before any intervention, mean recall is **98% on TIMING
and 84% on CONSEQUENCE but 61% on REASON** — columns that record *why* a label
was assigned — and a single clause naming that second criterion lifts REASON to
86%, closing a 23-point gap to three points, while leaving the other subtypes
flat, replicated across **sixteen models from nine laboratories**. The clause is brittle: two wordings of the same criterion
fail in mirror image, one excusing simultaneous columns and the other flagging
entire tables, with no wording uniformly better across models.

Because every dataset here is a well-known public table, we run the released
memorisation checker of Bordt et al. (2024) across four models. They reproduce
**none of 675 data rows and none of 30 headers**, but up to **61% of the
leaking column names** — so we test the result by renaming every column, and
across 44 model-condition cells from eight models the median cost is **0.053
F1**. Both models carrying the headline are unaffected at C6 (−0.019, −0.022);
one model of eight is the clear exception. Renaming rules out recall keyed to
strings, not to meaning, so we also generate **twenty tables that have never
been published** — 840 columns, 120 positives injected by rule and verified on
every row — and re-run the full roster against an analysis plan fixed before any
table existed. **The definitional finding replicates and is larger**: the
subtype deficit is **+33.0** points (95% CI [+17.1, +49.6]) against +23.2 on the
public corpus, the one-sentence repair **+22.0** against +24.8, and all sixteen
models show a positive deficit. Detection above the correlation baseline
survives with the identical counts — 12 of 16 models at the primary condition
and 14 of 16 with the clause, on both corpora. What does not transfer is
absolute quality: best F1 falls 0.929 → 0.852, and the shortfall is concentrated
in exactly the models that do best on public data (**r = −0.951**). Part of the
*advantage* looks like recall; the definitional structure does not.

We also audit our own ground truth against its licensing quotations and
**withdraw eight of the original 76 labels**, including an entire proposed
mechanism, on the grounds that the sources do not say what we had them saying.

Triage is what this supports today, and the number is the contribution: a
model's flags put **48 of 306 columns — 16% — in front of a human reviewer, and
that 16% contains every documented leak** (40 of 40, recall 1.000).

---

## 1. Introduction

Every practitioner has met the model that scores 0.99 and is worthless. The
usual cause is a column that could not have existed when the prediction was
supposed to be made, or one that records why the label was assigned.

"Data leakage" names at least five distinct failures. Two rows describing the
same patient landing on both sides of a split is *group leakage*. Released
files whose train and test portions overlap is *contamination*. A row
identifier that happens to correlate with the outcome is an *identifier
artefact*. A preprocessing step fitted on the full dataset is *procedural
leakage*. And a feature whose value encodes the outcome is **feature-level
target leakage**.

They are usually discussed together and should not be. They have different
causes, different detection methods and different remedies. Group leakage is a
splitting problem. Contamination is a release-hygiene problem. Feature-level
target leakage survives every split, and detecting it requires knowing what a
column *means* — which is why statistical methods struggle with it, and why a
language model is a plausible instrument.

Three contributions.

**(1) A benchmark.** 15 datasets, 604 columns, 68 positives, each licensed by
a written record and audited against it (§4.7). Two strata,
reported separately, because the difference between "a source names this
column" and "we read a source's description" is a property of the labels and
not something to average away. [N §1, §2]

A **third stratum** holds external validation and is never pooled with the
other two: a sweep of four documentation cultures outside the archive the
instruments were written on, and the two admissible records it produced (§6.4).
One is post-cutoff for most of the roster.

**(2) Evidence that models detect what correlation cannot, on public and on
unseen data alike.** Best F1 0.929 against a tuned upper-bound baseline at
0.630, with 12 of 16 models exceeding that baseline at the primary condition
and 14 of 16 with the derivation clause; exact performance at the primary
condition on the held-out set; downstream, model-based cleaning recovers the
honest ceiling to within 0.024 F1 while the baseline misses in both directions.
The advantage is not an artefact of familiarity: on twenty tables generated
locally and never published (§8), 12 of 16 models exceed the same baseline
computed the same way, and 14 of 16 with the clause — the identical counts. It
is smaller there, best F1 falling from 0.929 to 0.852 and the best margin from
+0.288 to +0.187, and §8.4 reports what that costs the claim.
[N §5, §6, §7, §8; NE §1, §3, §5]

**(3) A characterisation of the residual failure.** The gap is definitional
rather than perceptual: models miss what the word "leakage" is not taken to
cover. We show this two ways — by closing a subtype gap with one sentence, and
by causing the failure on demand with a wording change, in either direction,
differently for different models. [N §6, §7]

We also report what did not work: a criterion that fails on held-out data
(§7.2), an order-averaging remedy withdrawn as a general claim
(§7.5), an under-powered ablation we decline to interpret (§6.1), and a
closed-world dictionary rule that under-fires by more than two orders of
magnitude (§4.4).

## 2. Scope and taxonomy

### 2.1 Definition

Let a dataset have target *y* and a stated **prediction point** *t* — the
moment at which the model is asked to produce a prediction in the intended
deployment. A column *x* exhibits **feature-level target leakage** with respect
to *(y, t)* if *x*'s recorded value could not be obtained, or would not have its
final recorded value, by an honest process running at *t*; or if *x*'s value was
an input to the process that assigned *y*.

Three consequences, each routinely elided:

* **Leakage is a property of the triple *(x, y, t)*, not of a column.**
  `discharge_disposition_id` is a leak when predicting 30-day readmission and
  an ordinary covariate when predicting length of stay.
* **Predictiveness is not leakage.** A column may be almost perfectly
  predictive and entirely legitimate. Correlation-based detectors conflate
  these; we report one as a baseline rather than a method.
* **The prediction point must be stated by someone.** It is not recoverable
  from the data. We state it for every dataset (Appendix C) so a reader can
  reject one rather than all.

### 2.2 Four mechanisms

| mechanism | the column… | example |
|---|---|---|
| **REASON** | was an input used to assign the label | `TWF`/`HDF`/`PWF`/`OSF` → `Machine failure` |
| **CONSEQUENCE** | exists *because* the outcome occurred | `body` (body recovery number) → `survived` |
| **TIMING** | is recorded after the prediction point | 1995 crime counts → 1995 violent-crime rate predicted from 1990 census |
| **UPSTREAM** | was computed by a process that consumed outcome information | declared; see below |

Corpus composition by subtype is in [N §1].

**A fifth mechanism was proposed and then withdrawn.** An earlier draft added
SURROGATE — *a prior estimate of the same target* — after models declined to
flag STUDENT's `G1`/`G2` and SUPPORT2's `prg2m`/`prg6m`. Auditing the corpus
against its own licensing quotes (§4.7) showed the category could not survive
its evidence. The Student Performance documentation says only that predicting
`G3` without `G1`/`G2` is *"more difficult … but much more useful"* — a claim
about difficulty and utility, not availability — and `G1`/`G2` genuinely
precede `G3`. SUPPORT2's estimates are documented as recorded **at day 3**,
which is the prediction point.

There is a real problem in the vicinity: a model fed a physician's survival
estimate predicts the physician, not the patient. But that is a claim about
what a model is *for*, not about whether a value could honestly be obtained,
and no source in this corpus states it. **We withdraw the category rather than
defend a label the evidence does not license**, and the eight affected columns
are now coded legitimate.

**UPSTREAM is declared but not separately measured.** It has no dedicated
condition and no separate evaluation. We report it as a taxonomy entry, not
a result.

### 2.3 Out of scope

Group leakage, train/test contamination, procedural leakage, identifier
artefacts. §4.4 shows these are the *only* failures the field currently
documents, which is why separating them matters.

---

## 3. Related work


### 3.1 The formulation, and what it left unbuilt

Leakage was given its modern formulation by Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich and
Stitelman (2012; KDD 2011), who defined it in terms of *legitimacy* — a feature
is legitimate if it is available at the prediction point — and proposed the
**learn–predict separation** as the avoidance discipline. The canonical examples
come from the same group's competition post-mortems (Rosset et al., 2010), where
a patient identifier carried the outcome of the KDD Cup 2008 task.

That work is about avoiding leakage in data you collected. This paper is about
detecting it in data somebody else published, and the two differ in what is
available to the practitioner: not the collection process, but a table and its
documentation. Kaufman et al. supply the definition we adopt in §2.1 and no
corpus against which a detector could be scored, because scoring one was not
their problem. **The missing evaluand is the gap this paper fills**: column-level
labels, each licensed by a quotation from the dataset's own source, with a
measured instrument on top.

### 3.2 Scale

Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) surveyed leakage across **17 scientific fields and
294 affected papers** and proposed a taxonomy of eight leakage types. Field-level
studies reach the same conclusion independently: Roberts et al. (2021) screened
2,212 COVID-19 imaging studies and found **none clinically usable**, with leakage
among the recurring causes; Varoquaux and Cheplygina (2022) and Whalen et al.
(2021) report the pattern in medical imaging and genomics.

Their eight types are a *survey* taxonomy spanning fields and failure modes. Our
four mechanisms (§2.2) are a *coding* taxonomy for exactly one of theirs — **L2,
"model uses features that are not legitimate"** — cut for codability against a
written source rather than for coverage. §2.2 gives the mapping explicitly
rather than leaving a reader to construct it.

**L2 is the one type they decline to decompose.** Their other categories carry
sub-types; L2 does not, and the reason they give is that judging a feature's
legitimacy requires domain knowledge and is specific to the problem. That is a
fair description of the difficulty and it is the difficulty this paper attacks:
§2.2's four mechanisms are sub-categories of L2, and §4's protocol is an attempt
to make the judgment turn on a written source rather than on the coder's domain
knowledge. Whether it succeeds is what §4.7 and §7.1 are about.

Their remedy for L2 is expert review of the feature set. Ours does not replace
it — §10 argues the defensible product is triage, putting **48 of 306 columns,
16%,** in front of that expert instead of all of them.

### 3.3 What existing tooling targets

Data-validation systems check schemas and distributions: TFX data validation
(Breck et al., 2019) and Deequ (Schelter et al., 2018) express constraints over
*values*. Neither expresses a constraint over a column's relationship to a
target, because that relationship is not a property of the data — a column of
integers is legitimate or not depending on when it was written down. Sculley et
al. (2015) name the surrounding condition, *data dependencies* and *undeclared
consumers*, without proposing a detector.

The most recent dedicated tooling makes the point sharpest. **LeakageDetector**
(arXiv:2503.14723; 2.0 at ICSME 2025, arXiv:2509.15971) is a static analyser for
notebook pipelines, and it detects exactly three things: **overlap,
preprocessing, and multi-test leakage**. All three are procedural — the leak is
in the code, and reading the code finds it. A feature-level target leak is
invisible to any analysis of the pipeline, because the pipeline is correct: the
column is split cleanly, scaled after the split, and used once. What is wrong is
what the column *means*, and that lives in the documentation, not the program.

We are not aware of an annotated, column-level corpus of target-leaking features
prior to this one, under any of six search phrasings (§3.5).

### 3.4 LLMs over tabular schemas, and the contamination risk

Language models have been applied to tabular tasks that are semantic rather than
statistical: data wrangling and integration (Narayan et al., 2022) and few-shot
classification from serialised rows (Hegselmann et al., 2023). Deciding whether
`boat` was recorded before or after a shipwreck is a task of the same kind — it
is answered from what the column name and its documentation *mean*, and not from
the values.

The direct threat to that reading is **Bordt et al. (2024)**, who show that
language models have memorised many popular tabular datasets verbatim, with
contamination concentrating in datasets with meaningful column names — precisely
our setting. We take this as a measurement problem rather than a rhetorical one
and run their released checker against four models on all fifteen of our tables
(§6.3), alongside a renaming control of our own. The results cut both ways and
we report both: **no model reproduced any of 675 data rows or any of 30
headers**, but column names are recalled substantially, up to 61% of the leaking
ones. A concurrent framework for tabular contamination (arXiv:2510.20351) is
identified but unread at the time of writing and is not relied on here.

### 3.5 Two qualifications we would rather state than have inferred

**The term is overloaded.** Most recent work labelled "leakage benchmark" —
AntiLeak-Bench, LessLeak-Bench, "Benchmarking Benchmark Leakage in LLMs"
(arXiv:2404.18824), Tab-MIA and others — concerns *benchmark contamination*,
training data leaking into evaluation sets. That is a different object, excluded
in §2.3, and it now dominates the search term. Our sense is the Kaufman one.

**Target leakage has been taxonomised before, and only one of its types is our
object.** Larsen and Becker (2021, ch. 24 of *Automated Machine Learning for
Business*, OUP) give **seven types of target leakage** under a deliberately
expansive definition — a target leak has occurred whenever "model performance
metrics are better than what is possible in a real-world scenario due to the
inclusion of illegitimate features", which they note "goes beyond the
conventional description, which focuses only on features that are not available
at the time of prediction".

That conventional description is their **type 1**, and it is the whole of what
this paper measures:

| their type | what it concerns | relation to this paper |
|---|---|---|
| **1. feature not available at prediction time** | a column's value does not exist yet | **our object.** §2.2's four mechanisms partition it by *why* |
| 2. evaluation set precedes training cases in time | validation protocol | procedural; excluded in §2.3 |
| 3. feature available but absent in the deployed population | who the model is run on | deployment validity, not the column–target relation |
| 4. feature outside the model's use case | problem framing | as above |
| 5. feature interacts with how the target was operationalised | target definition | measurement artefact |
| 6. target values obtained from outside sources | competition conduct | *external leakage* in Kaufman et al.'s term; excluded in §2.3 |
| 7. subjects knew their own target status | survey design | same-method bias |

So our four mechanisms **refine their type 1** rather than compete with their
seven. Theirs is a pedagogical chapter with an exercise, not a benchmark, an
evaluation or a detector; and their broader scope makes the point this paper
starts from — that the one type an automated detector can act on from
documentation alone is a single line in a list of seven, and it is the line
nobody has built an evaluand for. A full mapping is in Appendix J.

Two further papers are adjacent without overlapping. Bendinelli et al. (2025)
put LLM agents on tabular *cleaning* — sensor faults, entry errors, integration
mistakes — with no leakage ground truth. And "LLM-Guided Automated Feature
Engineering for Time Series Data with Temporal Leakage Control" (*AI* 7(7), 245)
couples LLMs to explicit temporal availability constraints, the closest published
analogue to our C2 condition; if it operationalises availability as our models
do, it is independent support for §10's claim that availability and admissibility
come apart.

## 4. Benchmark construction

### 4.1 Evidence protocol

A column becomes a positive only with a **verbatim quotation of ≤25 words**
from a citable source, plus a locator. Explicitly inadmissible: our own
judgement, correlation with the target, feature importance, and a language
model's opinion. A candidate without a quotable licensing phrase is written to
a reject file and counted as attrition, not discarded silently.

Source formality is **not** an admission criterion — an uploader's paragraph
counts the same as a peer-reviewed codebook. What is required is that the
statement names the column and reaches a conclusion about it.

**Six positives predate this protocol** and do not meet it: TITANIC's `boat`
and `body` and COMPAS's four `r_*` fields were coded in the project's first
week, and their documentation was not retrievable from the run environment when
the records were backfilled. They carry a citation, a locator and an exact check
in the data, but no quotation, and they are marked E3 (§4.2.1). We report them
rather than dropping them, and a reader who rejects the tier can subtract six
positives from the corpus and re-read every table; no conclusion in this paper
turns on them.

### 4.2 Two strata

The corpus is split by **how each half was built**, not by how strong its
evidence turned out to be. Explicitness is a property of an individual record,
and it is counted separately in §4.2.1.

**Stratum A — the main corpus.** 12 datasets, 306 columns, **40 positives**
after the audit (§4.7). A source describes the column; we judge that the
description places it after the prediction point or shows it fed the label.
[N §1]

| dataset | cols | pos | target |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI4I | 10 | 4 | `Machine failure` |
| BANK | 16 | 1 | `y` |
| BONEMARROW | 36 | 5 | `survival_status` |
| COMPAS | 15 | 4 | `two_year_recid` |
| DIABETES | 47 | 1 | `readmitted` |
| ECHO | 12 | 1 | `alive_at_1` |
| HEARTFAIL | 12 | 1 | `DEATH_EVENT` |
| KOI | 40 | 4 | `koi_disposition` |
| LC | 29 | 2 | `loan_status` |
| STEEL | 33 | 6 | `Other_Faults` |
| SUPPORT2 | 47 | 9 | `death` |
| TITANIC | 9 | 2 | `survived` |
| **total** | **306** | **40** | |

**Stratum B — the transfer set.** 3 datasets, 298 columns, 28 positives, built
under one admission rule: the source itself must name the column — stating that
the target was summed from it, filing it under an outcome heading, or telling
the reader to predict without it.

| dataset | rows | cols | pos | subtypes | target |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CRIME (UCI 211) | 2,215 | 144 | 17 | REASON 8, TIMING 9 | `violentPerPop` |
| MI (UCI 579) | 1,700 | 122 | 11 | CONSEQUENCE 11 | `ZSN` |
| STUDENT (UCI 320) | 649 | 32 | 0 | both withdrawn (§4.7) | `G3` |

STUDENT now contributes **32 columns and no positives**. We keep it rather than
drop it: a dataset on which the correct answer is "nothing here leaks" is the
only direct measurement of a detector's false-positive behaviour that this
corpus contains.

Every Stratum-B quotation is verified against the cached source text at build
time and every column against the real CSV header; a misquote or a renamed
column raises rather than entering the ground truth.

Stratum B is a **genuine held-out set**: its selection criterion — "the source
already says so" — is independent of any model's behaviour, and none of its
datasets contributed a word to any prompt.

#### 4.2.1 What the evidence actually is

All 68 positives carry a written record, and most quote their source verbatim.
The six that do not are TITANIC `boat`/`body` and the four COMPAS `r_*` fields,
whose documentation was not retrievable from the run environment. Those six are
marked E3 and rest on the column's documented name plus an exact check in the
data (§4.3.1); they are the weakest evidence in the corpus and are labelled so.
Tier and explicitness counts are in [N §2].

The explicitness split does not follow the stratum split, because four
main-corpus positives turn out to be source-named after all. AI4I's UCI record states, in a sentence the sieve
missed and a hand reading found (§4.3.2), that the target *is set* from the
failure-mode columns. The construction split and the evidence split are
different cuts, and reporting them as one would overstate the transfer test.

### 4.3 Why the corpus had to be hand-built

We swept both machine-readable repositories of tabular datasets in full: **689
UCI records — the entire archive index — and 6,420 active OpenML descriptions,
7,109 in total.** Three passes ran over every text field, not just the data
dictionary: WARN sentences ("should be discarded", "not known before"), DEFINE
sentences ("the target was calculated using the sum of…"), and outcome
*headings*. Every hit was read.

| | UCI | OpenML |
|---|---|---|
| records swept | 689 | 6,420 |
| sieve actually applied | WARN \| DEFINE | **STRONG** (narrower — see below) |
| sentences surviving the sieve | 81 (13 datasets) | 89 (89 datasets; **10 distinct**) |
| **feature-level target leakage** | **6** | **0** frozen sieve · **1** corrected (2 columns) |
| group leakage | 0 | 2 |
| train/test contamination | 0 | 1 |
| identifier column | 3 | 2 |
| sieve false positive | 4 | 5 |

**Frozen-sieve rate: 6 in 7,109 — 0.084%. Corrected rate: 7 in 7,109 —
0.098%.** Both are reported because they answer different questions: the first
is what the instruments as frozen found, and is the number the sieve code in the
artefact bundle produces when re-run; the second is what the archive contains
once a defect in those instruments is repaired. Appendix B reports the
frozen-sieve figure, as it should. [N §4]

**The two columns of that table were not produced by the same instrument, and an
earlier version of this paper reported the OpenML cell as zero.** The record
that breaks that zero is Klaverjas2018, and it is worth more than a correction:
its two columns are documented, missed by almost every model, *and* worth
nothing downstream. It is dissected in §6.4.5. `explicit_scan`
(UCI) admits on **WARN | DEFINE**; `openml_scan` admits on a narrower **STRONG**
regex requiring *removed / dropped / discarded / excluded*, recording WARN only
as an after-the-fact flag. Re-running the *UCI* sieve over the cached OpenML
descriptions — 6,418 of the 6,420, the two lost to a fetch failure — yields
**145 sentences across 101 datasets** rather than 89 across 89 — so **137 sentences matched the UCI sieve and were never classified**.
Both sentence splitters were checked against each other and give identical
counts, so the gap is the admission gate and nothing else.

Reading those 137 recovers exactly one admissible record. OpenML **41228,
Klaverjas2018**, states in its uploader description:

> The fields `leaf_count` and `time_real` are meta-data as result from the
> αβ-search procedure, and **should not be used as predictors**.

"should not be used **as predictors**" is WARN vocabulary and not STRONG
vocabulary — the uploader wrote *not be used* where STRONG requires
*removed/dropped/discarded/excluded* — so the sentence was discarded before
anything classified it. The same description names the target (`outcome`) and
the 32 legitimate `card_*` columns explicitly, leaving no interpretation to do.
The remainder of the 137 are identifier warnings, batch metadata, and three
copies of a Student Performance sentence already withdrawn by the §4.7 audit.

This is a methods defect rather than a missed record, and it cuts against the
paper: the scarcity figure was too low, and it was too low because two archives
were swept with different gates and reported under one row label.

OpenML's ten distinct leakage sentences concern duplicate `patient_nbr`,
duplicate `obj_ID`, a train/test overlap, `serviceID`, a YouTube video `id`, and
five sieve false positives — one of which matched the trigger word *cheating*
because it is a **column name** (*central heating*) in a Munich rent index.

Every OpenML sentence the **STRONG** sieve surfaced uses "leakage" for splits or
identifiers, and none for a feature-level relationship; the one feature-level
record in the archive was surfaced only by the wider UCI gate, above. The sieve has
demonstrably imperfect recall (§4.3.2), so this bounds what it found rather
than what is there. There was no corpus to evaluate a detector on, so
we built one. This is stated as a measurement rather than an assertion, and it
is the justification for §4.1's expense, not the paper's finding.

Two design points, both forced by failures:

* **Reading only per-variable descriptions is structurally blind.** The
  archive's two most-cited warnings — Bank Marketing's `duration` and Student
  Performance's `G1`/`G2` — live in free prose. Our first pass read only the
  dictionary and found neither.
* **A derivation sieve must know the target's name.** Requiring the literal
  words *class*/*label*/*target* as the sentence subject fired **zero** times in
  689 datasets; authors write "The per capita violent crimes variable was
  calculated using…".

#### 4.3.1 Coded derivations checked against the data

A label read off documentation is an inference, and an inference can be wrong.
Where a coded mechanism implies a testable pattern in the values, we check it.
The check is not what makes a label true — a legitimate column can correlate
perfectly by accident, which is precisely why correlation is a baseline here
and not an oracle — but a coded derivation the data contradict is withdrawn.

| dataset | implied pattern | result |
|---|---|---|
| COMPAS | `r_*` populated only when `is_recid` | exact, 1.0000 |
| AI4I | each flag ⇒ target set | 4 of 5 exact; **`RNF` refuted** |
| KOI | any false-positive flag ⇒ `FALSE POSITIVE` | 0.9958 vs 0.0198 |
| TITANIC | `boat` ⇔ survived; `body` ⇒ died | 0.9756; 0 of 121 survived |
| DIABETES | terminal discharge ⇒ no 30-day readmission | 0.0177 vs 0.1139 |

[N §3]

The refutation is the useful one. AI4I's documentation names **five** failure
modes as inputs to `Machine failure`; in the table, `RNF` sets the target in 1
of its 19 flagged rows. `RNF` is therefore coded legitimate **against its own
source**, and the four confirmed flags are the positives. Source-named ground
truth is stronger than inferred ground truth, and it still has to be checked.

#### 4.3.2 A demonstrated miss, and what it bounds

Two fetch passes had left 29 of the archive's 689 records undownloaded, and the
sweep reported 660 as though it were the archive. Re-fetching them for the
appendix turned up AI4I 2020 (UCI 601) — a dataset already inside this
benchmark — whose documentation reads:

> If at least one of the above failure modes is true, the process fails and the
> 'machine failure' label is set to 1.

That is an explicit, source-authored, feature-level target-leakage statement,
and all three sieve families miss it. Each requires a preposition after the
assignment verb (*derived from*, *determined by*); this author wrote a
conditional (*set to 1*, governed by a preceding *if*).

Editing the sieve and reporting the result as a sieve find would be fitting the
instrument to its answer. The original sieve is left frozen, and a
one-pattern extension runs beside it over all 7,109 records. It recovers
exactly the sentence above and one other construction — two OpenML records
describing image annotation, not leakage. Adding it to the corrected rate gives
**8 in 7,109, 0.113%**. [N §4]

The three figures stack in one direction only — 6 from the frozen sieve, 7 once the
OpenML gate is repaired, 8 once one further construction is admitted — and
every step is a *miss* being recovered, never a hit being withdrawn. All three
are lower bounds, and the misses are the proof: a sieve is a lexical
instrument, and authors who do document a derivation are not obliged to phrase
it the way the instrument expects. What the sweep licenses is narrower: across
7,109 records the sieves surfaced **eight** feature-level leakage
statements, which is too few to assemble a benchmark from and is the only claim
§4.3 needs. It does not license a claim about how rare leakage itself is, nor
about what a different instrument would find.

### 4.4 A negative result: the closed-world dictionary rule

Before the sweep we tried to avoid the expense. If a dataset documents *every*
column, then silence is informative: a column the dictionary does not describe
as post-outcome can be presumed clean. **406 of the archive's 689 datasets meet
that condition**, covering 25,697 columns.

Applied to all of them, the rule flags **23 columns — 0.090%** — against a
base rate of 11.3% in this benchmark's hand-coded corpus. On the eleven corpus
datasets that fall inside its scope it recovers **8 of 56 positives (14.3%)**.
[N §15]

Where it works, it works for a clear reason: BONEMARROW's dictionary literally
says *"Time taken for platelet recovery"*, and the rule gets 5 of 5. Where it
fails, it fails for an equally clear one. `discharge_disposition_id` is
documented as *"Integer identifier corresponding to 29 distinct values, for
example, discharged to home, expired, and not available"* — a complete,
accurate description that never says the field records an outcome. STEEL's six
sibling faults, CRIME's seventeen crime counts and MI's eleven complications are
each described impeccably and individually; what makes them leak is their
relationship to the target, which no per-column description states.

**A complete data dictionary is not documented provenance.** This is the
negative result that forced the corpus to be hand-built, and it is also the
clearest statement of what the task actually requires: not reading a
description, but relating it to a target.

### 4.5 Attrition, and one instructive recovery

The corpus-expansion round adjudicated **11 candidate datasets and rejected 136
candidate rows**: 120 for having no licensing phrase at all, 12 because the
phrase was in a neighbouring dictionary row rather than the column's own, and 4
for prose context without an unambiguous statement. **Five datasets yielded
admissible evidence; six yielded none** (`actg175`, `credit`, `ctg`, `mi`,
`polish`, `wpbc`). [N §2]

The zero-evidence six look like a finding — their literature never states when
these columns were recorded — and one of them shows how far that reading can be
trusted. Myocardial Infarction Complications is in the list. Its evidence is a
*heading*, `Complications and outcomes of myocardial infarction:`, standing over
attributes 113–124, and every sieve we had at the time read sentences. Adding a
heading-aware pass recovered **eleven positives from a dataset recorded as
undocumented**, and MI is now the second-largest contributor to Stratum B.

**The attrition set was partly measuring the shape of our instrument, not the
silence of the sources.** The same caution applies to §4.3's sweep, where §4.3.2
gives a second, independent demonstration of it.

### 4.6 Legitimate-by-default

A column with no source statement is scored legitimate. Reported **precision is
therefore a lower bound**: a model flagging a genuine but undocumented leak is
counted wrong. §7.4 shows this is not hypothetical.

### 4.7 Auditing the ground truth against its own quotations

Building the corpus quote-first does not make it correct. It makes it
*checkable*, which is different, and the check had not been run. Asked whether
a prior estimate of the target is really leakage, we went back and read every
licensing quote against the label it was supposed to license. **Eight of 76
labels did not survive.**

**The rule, fixed before the effect was measured.** A column leaves the ground
truth when its own documentation places its value **at or before the prediction
point**. Not when a model missed it, not when it looks arguable — when the
source says the value is already fixed when the prediction is made.

| dataset | columns | the documentation |
|---|---|---|
| SUPPORT2 | `sps`, `aps` | "SUPPORT physiology score **on day 3**"; "APACHE III **day 3** physiology score" |
| SUPPORT2 | `surv2m`, `surv6m` | "survival estimate **at day 3** (predicted by a model)" |
| SUPPORT2 | `prg2m`, `prg6m` | "Physician's 2-month survival estimate" |
| STUDENT | `G1`, `G2` | "G3 is the final year grade (issued at the 3rd period), while G1 and G2 correspond to the 1st and 2nd period grades" |

The prediction point for SUPPORT2 is study day 3. Six columns are documented as
fixed *at* it. `aps` is APACHE III — a published clinical severity index, not
fitted on this dataset's outcomes, and an ordinary covariate by any reading.

**How this happened is the part worth reporting.** All fifteen SUPPORT2
positives were licensed by a single sentence from a third-party paper:

> "we rigorously excluded surrogate outcomes and administrative features
> containing future information"

It names no column. One unnamed methodological sentence was doing the work of
fifteen records, while the dataset's own variable descriptions — better
evidence, freely available, and quoted in the table above — sat unread. The
nine SUPPORT2 columns that survive are now licensed from those descriptions
instead: `avtisst` is *"Average TISS score, **days 3-25**"*, a window running 22
days past the prediction point; `slos` is *"Days from Study Entry to
**Discharge**"*.

**The audit raises eight of the ten models it could be computed on, and
lowers two.** (The six Vertex models were run after the withdrawal and have no
pre-audit score, so the comparison does not extend to them.) The
withdrawn columns were disproportionately ones models declined to flag, so
removing them flatters models that were already precise and penalises the two
loosest, whose surplus false positives now weigh against a smaller positive
set: `Qwen3-Coder-480B` and `deepseek-v4-flash` both score lower after the
audit than before it. (Those deltas compare against a superseded scoring run
and are not reproducible from the current artefacts, so we give the direction
and not a magnitude.) We state the rule before the effect
and report both sets of numbers [N §1, §6]; a correction that flattered every
model uniformly would deserve more suspicion than one that does not. One check that the rule was not
reverse-engineered: `adlp` and `adls` are documented *"measured at day 3"* and
were **already** negatives before the audit existed.

**Why this is in the paper.** Not as a confession — as a statement of what the
artefact contains. A reader who thinks a physician's survival estimate *is*
inadmissible can put `prg2m` and `prg6m` back; the eight withdrawn columns are
named here and their quotations are in Appendix B, so that disagreement is
actionable rather than invisible. What a benchmark owes its users is not the
claim that its labels are beyond dispute, but enough information to dispute
them.

---

## 5. Experimental setup

### 5.1 Conditions

Each condition adds exactly one thing to the previous:

| | added |
|---|---|
| C0 | column names only (ill-posed control) |
| **C1** | **+ target column — primary condition** |
| C2 | + prediction point |
| C3 | + the dataset's own documented description |
| C4 | + five sample rows — **the ablation** |
| C5 | domain-expert scaffold |
| **C6** | **+ derivation criterion** |
| C7 | + surrogate criterion |
| **C9** | + derivation criterion **stated without reference to time** |

C4 is intended as the ablation that matters: if provenance were recoverable from
values, showing the model data should help. In the event it was run on too few
cells to settle anything (§6.1). C3 uses only author-written descriptions — one
we wrote could encode the answer.

C6's clause, in full:

> There are two distinct reasons a column can be UNAVAILABLE, and both count:
> (a) TIMING — the value does not exist, or is not yet final, at the prediction
> point. (b) DERIVATION — the value records WHY the target's outcome was
> assigned, or was itself an input used to determine the target. **This holds
> EVEN IF the value was recorded BEFORE the prediction point.** A column can
> satisfy (b) while being **chronologically earlier** than the target. Judging
> only by (a) will mark such a column AVAILABLE, which is wrong. Being merely
> predictive is not sufficient for either.

C9 replaces the emphasised sentences with an information test and forbids
temporal reasoning inside (b):

> (b) DERIVATION — the target's value is a function of this column's value…
> Criterion (b) is about INFORMATION, not about time. Do not test (b) by asking
> when the value was measured. Test it by asking: could the target be
> reconstructed, wholly or in part, from this column?

The two differ in exactly two hunks — five lines replaced by seven; the opening
sentence, clause (a) and the closing "merely predictive is not sufficient"
paragraph are byte-identical (Appendix D). **C6 states criterion (b) in temporal
vocabulary** (*"EVEN IF the value was recorded BEFORE the prediction point"*,
*"chronologically earlier"*), which is the vocabulary a literal reader can
construe narrowly. **C9 states criterion (b) with no temporal term in it at
all**, and mentions time only afterwards, to discharge it (*"whatever its
timing — earlier, later, or simultaneous"*).

### 5.2 Protocol

Whole-table prompting — provenance is relational; a column is judged against a
target alongside its siblings. Every column must be answered; `ABSTAIN` is
permitted and reported, because forcing binary verdicts inflates false
positives and hides calibration. A one-line reason per column is required; the
reasons are how §7.3's mechanism was identified.

**Column order is shuffled per run.** §7.5 shows ordering alone moves F1 by up
to 0.380 between two shuffles of the same prompt. [N §13]

Cells answering fewer than 90% of columns are excluded and counted. **Failed
API calls are never cached**: a quota error written to cache would become a
permanent zero-coverage "answer" the model never gave. Likewise, a cell whose
verdict keys do not intersect the truth keys is refused rather than scored —
scoring it yields zero recall, which is indistinguishable from a model that
found nothing.

**3,344 cells are cached** across six providers. Three counts appear in this
paper and they count different things, so each is named where it is used:
**3,344** cached in total, including the Stratum E, scale-ladder and
opaque-name arms (§8); of which **462** are paraphrase-arm cells with
aliased column names (§6.3); and **1,934** real-name Stratum A/B cells that
parse, which is the denominator of the coverage audit. Detection tables are
computed on the roster subset of that population; the opaque-name arm is
excluded from it entirely, its column names being `col_1…col_n` rather than
real ones. [N §10, §17]

### 5.3 Models, in two tiers

Sixteen models from nine laboratories, reported in **two tiers that answer
different questions**. Mixing them in one ranking would invite a comparison
neither tier supports.

**Frontier tier** — `claude-opus-5` (max effort), `gpt-5.6-sol` (extra-high),
`gemini-3.7-flash`, `gemini-3.5-flash`, and, on Vertex, `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`,
`gemini-2.5-pro`, `grok-4.20` and `grok-4.1-fast` each in a reasoning and a
non-reasoning variant. These carry the **detection** result:
what the best available instrument achieves. `claude-opus-5` and `gpt-5.6-sol`
were run through their chat interfaces with one sub-agent per cell; their
prompts were verified byte-identical to the API runs by regenerating and
hash-matching against cached cells.

**Replication tier** — `Kimi-K3`, `GLM-5.2`, `DeepSeek-V4-Pro`,
`deepseek-v4-flash`, `nemotron-3-super-120b`, `Qwen3-Coder-480B`, all
open-weight, all run at `reasoning_effort: high`. These carry the **mechanism**
result. A subtype signature found in four frontier models from three
laboratories could be a shared-training-data artefact; the same signature in
sixteen models from nine laboratories, at four parameter scales, is not.

The tiers are **not** a capability ranking, and one result forbids reading them
as one: `Kimi-K3` scores F1 0.876, above six of the ten
frontier models, and reaches it at C1 with no clause at all. We report it and
do not explain it away.

### 5.4 Baselines

All thresholds swept **on the answers**, making every baseline an upper bound.
Fitted on Stratum A: 306 columns, 40 positives. [N §5]

| baseline | P | R | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| B0 always AVAILABLE | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 |
| B1 name regex (frozen §4.3 vocabulary) | 0.667 | 0.100 | 0.174 |
| **B1-tuned** (vocabulary fitted to Stratum A) | 0.452 | 0.350 | **0.394** |
| B2 univariate AUC | 0.733 | 0.275 | 0.400 |
| **B3 \|correlation\|** | **0.697** | **0.575** | **0.630** |
| B4 missingness asymmetry | 0.667 | 0.150 | 0.245 |

Every threshold is swept on the answers, so each figure is an upper bound no
deployment could reach. B3 is the strongest and is the comparison used
throughout.

**B1-tuned exists because B1 is too weak to be a fair test.** B1 applies §4.3's
frozen sieve vocabulary — written for dictionary prose, never for names — and a
reader is entitled to ask whether a keyword rule *built for this job* would do
better. So we built one: 34 name patterns (`days_to_*`, `*_outcome`, `body`,
`discharge_*`, the fault siblings, and the rest, listed in Appendix E) chosen by
looking at which columns leak here. It reaches **F1 0.394**, more than double
B1's and still 0.52 below the best model, and it buys the recall with
precision — 17 false positives, among them ECHO's `survival`, DIABETES's
`admission_type_id` and `admission_source_id`, KOI's three `koi_duration*`
columns and LC's `grade`.

**Its Stratum B score is 0.000, and that is the more interesting number.** Not
one pattern was drawn from a Stratum B column, so Stratum B is a genuine
out-of-sample test — and the rule that recovers 14 of 40 positives on Stratum A
recovers **0 of 28** on Stratum B, where `gpt-5.6-sol` at C1 is exact. Leaking
column names share no vocabulary that transfers from one dataset to the next.
This is the direct answer to the memorisation reading of §6.3: if the models
were matching a learned vocabulary of leaky names, the rule that encodes exactly
such a vocabulary would not score zero where they score one. [N §5]

---

### 6.1 Models clear the statistical ceiling

Stratum A. Every condition comparison is **matched on cells**: C1 and C6 are
scored only on the (dataset, shuffle) pairs that exist in both arms, so the two
rows of a model describe the same column judgments. `ds` is the number of
datasets and `sd` the number of shuffles pooled. C9 is compared against C6 on
its own matched cells, in §7.3. [N §6]

**Frontier tier.**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **gpt-5.6-sol xhigh** | C1 | 0.854 | 0.875 | 0.864 | 12 | 1 |

and STUDENT at C1 and C6, plus KOI at C9 on the Vertex arm. The cause is an instrument interaction rather than our

**Replication tier** (open weights, `reasoning_effort: high`).

| model | cond | P | R | F1 | ds | sd |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kimi-K3 | C1 | 0.796 | 0.975 | 0.876 | 12 | 1 |
