## 7. Results: what the models miss

### 7.1 Held-out, source-named evaluation

Stratum B, up to 3 shuffles per cell. [N §7]

| model | cond | P | R | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **gpt-5.6-sol** | **C1** | **1.000** | **1.000** | **1.000** |
| | C2 | 0.706 | 1.000 | 0.828 |
| | C6 | 0.840 | 1.000 | 0.913 |
| | C9 | 0.904 | 0.893 | 0.898 |
| claude-opus-5 | C1 | 0.596 | **1.000** | 0.747 |
| | C2 | 0.556 | **1.000** | 0.715 |
| | **C6** | 0.706 | **1.000** | **0.828** |
| | C9 | 0.587 | **1.000** | 0.740 |
| gemini-3.5 †| C1 | 0.638 | 0.988 | 0.776 |
| | C6 | 0.689 | 0.976 | 0.808 |
| Qwen3-480B | C0 | 0.455 | 0.714 | 0.556 |
| | C1 | 0.358 | 0.905 | 0.514 |
| | C2 | 0.561 | 0.762 | 0.646 |
| | C6 | 0.451 | 0.869 | 0.593 |

**`gpt-5.6-sol` at C1 is exact.** 84 true positives, **zero** false positives
and **zero** false negatives across 894 column judgments — three shuffles of
298 columns — at the primary condition, from column names and a target alone.

**This is the paper's most quotable number and the least reproducible one, and
the two facts belong in the same paragraph.** `gpt-5.6-sol` and `claude-opus-5`
have no API key in our environment: every one of their cells was obtained by
hand through a chat interface, one sub-agent per cell, with the prompt
hash-matched to the API runs (§5.3). A reader cannot re-run them. The effort
settings are vendor labels rather than versioned artefacts, and the models
behind those labels can change under us without notice. We date the runs in
Appendix D and report the figure as what a frontier model did on a given day,
not as a reproducible constant.

It is tempting to read this as an independent audit of the ground truth — a
frontier model, given no documentation, no prediction point and no derivation
clause, reproducing the source-stated labels of a held-out set exactly. **We do
not make that claim, because it is circular in the direction that flatters us.**
`gpt-5.6-sol` is one of the systems under evaluation. Using its agreement as
evidence that the labels are right, and then reporting its score as evidence
that the models are good, licenses each from the other.

The non-circular reading is weaker and is the one we hold: the labels and the
model may share a common cause. Stratum B's positives are named by their own
sources in ordinary technical English, and a model trained on ordinary technical
English will read those names the same way a coder does. Exact agreement is then
evidence that **Stratum B is lexically easy**, not that the coding is correct —
which is consistent with REASON scoring 24/24 at every condition including C0
(§7.2), where the model is given nothing but column names. What would break the
tie is a second reader who is not a language model, and we do not have one.

Opus reaches **recall 1.000 at every condition** on the same set and pays for it
in precision.

### 7.2 The derivation clause moves a different subtype than expected

§6.2's account of C6 was that it lifts REASON and leaves other subtypes flat.
That account does not survive Stratum B. On Stratum B,
**REASON is 24/24 = 100% in every condition of every model except one** —
including C0, which is given nothing but column names and not even a target.
The exception is treated below. `murders`,
`rapes`, `robberies` against `violentPerPop` are lexically transparent, so there
is no gap for the clause to close. All movement is elsewhere: it is CONSEQUENCE
that varies wildly here, from 0% to 100% across models. [N §7]

The single exception is `nemotron-3-super` at C6, where REASON falls to 11/24 —
but so does everything else (TIMING 0/27, CONSEQUENCE 2/33, F1 0.226). That is a
model failing on a prompt, not a subtype effect, and we count it as neither.

We state the §6.2 reading and its failure rather than replacing it with the
Stratum B result and presenting that as what we meant. What survives is
narrower: the derivation criterion moves whichever subtype a model was already
missing, and on this corpus that was not REASON. A mechanism-specific claim
about C6 is not supportable on the evidence we have.

### 7.3 The intervention is brittle in both directions

C9 was written from a diagnosis, and the hypothesis it was meant to test was
fixed in writing before any C9 cell ran (`REGISTERED_C9.md`, shipped unedited in
the artefact bundle).

**The diagnosis.** DeepSeek-V4-Pro flags all six of STEEL's sibling fault
columns at C1 and un-flags all six at C6, with the identical stated reason each
time: **"measured concurrently."** Those six define the target — `Other_Faults`
is 1 exactly when all six are 0 — so they are the clearest REASON case in the
corpus. Like-for-like, REASON falls 10/15 → 8/15 (67% → 53%) at unchanged
recall, and precision falls with it — 0.627 → 0.457, false positives 19 → 38.
C6 made this model worse on both axes, so the diagnosis does not rest on the
scores. It rests on the reason the model gives: the same six columns, flagged
and then un-flagged, with the same six words. The hypothesis was that C6's most
emphatic sentence argues timing is irrelevant *in the vocabulary of timing*, so
a literal reader concludes "simultaneous" falls outside the rule.

**Confirmed.** Under C9, DeepSeek-V4-Pro recovers **6/6 on STEEL**, reasoning
*"true label for another fault type; not available when predicting
Other_Faults"* — a statement about what the value *is*, not when it was taken.
Its main-corpus F1 rises 0.582 → **0.772**, its best cell in any condition.

**But C9 is not uniformly better.** Across seven models with all three
conditions:

| model | F1 C6 | F1 C9 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro | 0.582 | **0.772** | **+0.190** |
| claude-opus-5 | 0.909 | **0.929** | +0.020 |
| Kimi-K3 | 0.882 | **0.896** | +0.014 |
| deepseek-v4-flash | 0.711 | 0.711 | 0.000 |
| GLM-5.2 | **0.871** | 0.860 | −0.011 |
| nemotron-3-super | **0.690** | 0.654 | −0.036 |
| gpt-5.6-sol | **0.918** | 0.857 | −0.061 |

Each row is matched on its own cells: a model's C6 figure here is scored on the
(dataset, shuffle) pairs that also have a C9 answer, which is why some differ
from §6.1. [N §6]

**The two wordings fail in mirror image.** C6's temporal carve-out lets a
literal reader excuse a simultaneous column. C9's reconstruction test has no
brake: on AI4I — a synthetic dataset whose target is a threshold rule over its
sensors — `gpt-5.6-sol` flagged **all ten columns**, reasoning that each is *"an
input to the synthetic rules that determine Machine failure."* True, and
useless. GPT's TIMING recall also fell 27/27 → 18/27 on Stratum B, the
mechanism running in reverse.

**On the held-out set, C9 mostly buys precision and spends recall.** Matched on
(dataset, shuffle) exactly as §6 matches Stratum A, eight models have cells at
both conditions on Stratum B. Precision improves in **six of eight** and false
positives fall in **six of eight**, several of them sharply —
`gemini-3.1-pro-preview` 0.755 → 0.913 with false positives 27 → 8 while recall
*rises* to 1.000, and `gemini-2.5-pro` 0.352 → 0.467 with 136 → 73. But F1 is a
wash: four up, four down, mean **+0.006**. The clause is not making these models
better; it is moving them along a precision–recall trade, and where recall was
already high the trade is worth taking.

| model | P C6 → C9 | false positives | R C6 → C9 | ΔF1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gemini-3.1-pro-preview | 0.755 → **0.913** | 27 → 8 | 0.988 → 1.000 | +0.099 |
| grok-4.20-non-reasoning | 0.535 → **0.684** | 46 → 25 | 0.631 → 0.643 | +0.083 |
| gemini-2.5-pro | 0.352 → **0.467** | 136 → 73 | 0.881 → 0.762 | +0.076 |
| grok-4.1-fast-reasoning | 0.452 → **0.543** | 85 → 53 | 0.833 → 0.750 | +0.044 |
| grok-4.20-reasoning | 0.507 → **0.619** | 68 → 32 | 0.833 → 0.619 | −0.012 |
| gpt-5.6-sol | 0.840 → **0.904** | 16 → 8 | 1.000 → 0.893 | −0.015 |
| claude-opus-5 | 0.706 → 0.587 | 35 → **59** | 1.000 → 1.000 | −0.087 |
| grok-4.1-fast-non-reasoning | 0.628 → 0.522 | 29 → **32** | 0.583 → 0.417 | −0.141 |

Opus is one of the two exceptions, and it is the sharpest single case: on
Stratum A, C9 raises its precision to 0.886, its best; on Stratum B it *lowers*
precision from 0.706 to 0.587 at identical subtype recall, changing nothing but
false positives (35 → 59). **The same clause, the same model, opposite
directions on two corpora.** An earlier version of this section generalised the
held-out behaviour from Opus and `gpt-5.6-sol`; matched, those two are the
minority, and the majority direction is the opposite one. [N §7]

**No wording of the derivation criterion is uniformly better, and we can name
the failure mode of each.** C6 excuses simultaneous columns to a literal
reader; C9 has no brake on reconstruction. Both are visible in the reasons the
models give, not only in the scores. Prompt-level interventions for this task
require per-deployment validation, which no current practice provides.

### 7.4 What the leakage costs

Four-plus arms differing **only** in which columns are present — no tuning, no
per-arm choices. Group-aware 5-fold splits where a unit repeats
(`patient_nbr`, `member_id`, `id`). Class-balanced learners with real capacity;
the decision threshold is chosen inside each outer fold on out-of-fold
predictions over the *training* part only, so no test fold helps choose its own
threshold. The identical procedure runs in every arm. [N §8]

**Honest ceiling (arm GT), to establish the downstream models are sound:**

F1 ranges **0.610–0.943** across 12 datasets (rf); ten of twelve exceed 0.66.
BONEMARROW is the exception at 0.629 with AUC 0.621 — see below. [N §8]

**BONEMARROW is excluded from the downstream headline and kept in the detection
headline, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight.** The two are
different axes — the point §6.4.5, §6.4.8 and §7.5 make with Klaverjas, CKD and
ECHO — and a record can fail on one while standing on the other. Its ΔF1 is
degenerate because the cleaned arm has almost no signal left, which says nothing
about whether its five positives are correctly coded: each is licensed by the
dictionary's own wording (§4.4 recovers 5 of 5 there). Dropping it from
detection because its downstream number is uninformative would be exactly the
conflation this paper argues against.

**Inflation = metric(all columns) − metric(documented positives removed):**

| learner | mean ΔF1 | median | max | mean ΔAUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| random forest | **0.145** | 0.141 | 0.304 | 0.129 |
| gradient boosting | 0.130 | 0.123 | 0.304 | 0.128 |
| rf, excluding BONEMARROW | 0.130 | 0.133 | 0.304 | 0.109 |
| gb, excluding BONEMARROW | 0.116 | 0.116 | 0.304 | 0.105 |

**ΔF1 exceeds ΔAUC**, and the two are not redundant in either direction. AI4I
shows ΔF1 0.207 against ΔAUC 0.015 — the four failure-mode flags barely change
ranking quality and massively change the operating point. BANK and LC invert it
(ΔF1 0.005 and 0.056 against ΔAUC 0.140 and 0.187). An AUC-only evaluation would
have called AI4I clean.

Confusion matrices (pooled over folds) make the mechanism concrete. COMPAS
leaked: **3 false negatives out of 2,809 positives**, recall 0.999 — the model
reads the answer off `r_offense_date`, which exists only if recidivism
occurred. Cleaned, it misses 487. AI4I leaked: **zero false positives across
9,661 true negatives**, because `TWF/HDF/PWF/OSF` are OR-ed to make the target
— the derivation the dataset's own documentation states (§4.3.2). [N §9]

**Does model-based cleaning reach the ceiling?** Residual = arm − GT; ~0 means
the arm removed what mattered.

| arm | mean residual F1 | mean \|residual\| |
|---|---|---|
| ALL (do nothing) | +0.147 | 0.147 |
| claude-opus-5 | −0.024 | **0.024** |
| gpt-5.6-sol | −0.024 | **0.024** |
| gemini-3.7 | −0.023 | 0.024 |
| gemini-3.5 †| −0.023 | 0.023 |
| Qwen3-480B | −0.022 | 0.023 |
| B3 baseline | −0.024 | **0.048** |
| GT (the ceiling) | 0.000 | 0.000 |

Every model lands within 0.024 of the ceiling; residuals are slightly negative,
so nothing measurable is left behind. **B3 matches on the mean by cancellation**
— its absolute error is twice as large, because it under-drops on some datasets
and over-drops on others, and the two errors average out.

Two datasets show both halves of that cancellation:

* **LC.** B3's threshold (|r| ≥ 0.3202) drops `recoveries` (|r| = 0.340) and
  keeps `collection_recovery_fee` (|r| = 0.205), which is the amount recovered
  by the collection agency after the loan charged off. The arm scores **F1
  0.956 against a ceiling of 0.907** — still inflated, because it kept a leak.
* **TITANIC.** B3 drops `sex` (|r| = 0.529, entirely legitimate and the single
  most useful feature on the table) and keeps `body` (|r| = 0.014), the body
  identification number — a column that exists only for passengers whose bodies
  were recovered, and therefore only for the dead. The arm scores **F1 0.658
  against a ceiling of 0.722** — now below it, because it deleted signal and
  kept a leak.

`body` is the cleanest statement of the problem in the corpus: a column whose
value is a direct consequence of the outcome and whose linear correlation with
that outcome is 0.014. No correlation threshold can find it at any setting that
does not also delete `sex`. A correlation threshold cannot separate *correlated
because it caused the label* from *correlated because it predicts the label*,
and it cannot see a leak that is not correlated at all.

**Over-flagging has a measurable cost, and one dataset shows it.** On ECHO —
131 rows, the smallest table in the corpus — all five measured models drop
**two** columns where the ground truth drops one, and F1 falls to **0.407**
against the documented cleaning's 0.677. At that sample size one extra deletion
is expensive.

**We call that 0.677 a benchmark rather than a ceiling, because on ECHO it is
not one.** Keeping every column scores **0.684** under the same learner, so the
documented cleaning *costs* 0.006 F1 here — ECHO is a second documented-inert
case alongside Klaverjas (§6.4.5). Under gradient boosting the sign flips and
cleaning gains 0.021 (0.721 → 0.742). One dataset in the corpus whose leak is
worth nothing to remove, and whose sign depends on the learner, is a reason to
report ΔF1 per dataset and per learner throughout and never as a single number
[N §12]. It is the
clearest case in the corpus of a detector being wrong in the direction that a
triage product must avoid, and it is why §10 argues for review rather than
autonomous deletion.

**The audit barely moved these numbers, which is itself informative.**
Withdrawing eight labels changed detection scores by up to 0.061 and left mean
ΔF1 unchanged at 0.147 (rf) and 0.130 (gb), because the withdrawn columns were
largely ones the models did not flag: neither the ceiling nor the model arms
shifted.

**This test cannot detect leaks our ground truth also missed.** If a genuine
leak is absent from both the model's flags and the documented set, both arms
are inflated identically and the residual is zero. It shows the model agrees
with us, not that we are right. Weak positive evidence: cleaned performance is
domain-plausible (COMPAS AUC 0.725, DIABETES 0.685, LC 0.742).

**BONEMARROW's cleaned arm is degenerate, not merely weak** — TN falls to 6 of
102 while recall rises to 0.976, precision 0.464 on a 45% base rate. It has
stopped discriminating. 187 rows and 36 features after removing 5 columns is
below what the method supports; we report it separately and exclude it from the
headline mean.

### 7.5 Negative results and instability

**Order sensitivity is a model property, not a task property.** Per-seed F1
spread on Stratum B at C1: `gpt-5.6-sol` **0.000** — three shuffles, one answer —
against `claude-opus-5` 0.132 and Qwen-480B **0.302**. The largest spread we
measure is 0.380 (gemini-3.5, Stratum B, C6), which is larger than any
difference between conditions for that model. Stratum A is calmer but not calm:
gemini-3.5 spans 0.071 at C1 while Qwen spans 0.190. [N §13]

On Qwen, CONSEQUENCE recall on one dataset runs 27% / 100% / 100% across three
shuffles of the same 122 column names with nothing else changed.

We proposed majority-voting over shuffles as a remedy. It does **not**
generalise: `gpt-5.6-sol` returns an identical answer under three shuffles
(spread 0.000), so there is nothing to average, and any gain is confined to
models whose answers vary. **We withdraw the general claim.** [N §13]

**C4 and C5 can hurt.** On Qwen, C4 (sample rows) contains everything C2 has
and still loses C2's CONSEQUENCE gain, and C5 drives two datasets to F1 0.000.
These are single-shuffle cells against a measured spread of 0.302 for this
model on this stratum, so we report the direction and not a magnitude.

---

## 8. Results: does any of this survive on tables the models have not seen?

Every dataset in Strata A–D is public and almost certainly in pretraining.
Stratum B is held out from **prompt development**, not from training data;
Strata C and D are external to us, not to the models. So no stratum reported so
far separates *the model reasoned about this table* from *the model recalls this
table*. The paraphrase control (§6.3) rules out **string-keyed** recall — name,
target, columns and sample keys renamed together, and `claude-opus-5` goes
0.905 → 0.916 — but its authoring rule preserves transparency level, so
`koi_period` → `tc_orbper` still means orbital period, and semantic retrieval
survives it.

A single account therefore fits every number above: the models have memorised
facts about these tables, C1 fails to cue the right retrieval, and the C6 clause
cues it. This section exists to break that tie.

### 8.1 Stratum E: twenty tables that have never been published

Twenty tables generated locally by a committed generator at a fixed seed, **840
columns, 120 injected positives — exactly 40 REASON, 40 CONSEQUENCE, 40
TIMING** — and not published anywhere until every model run was complete. Leak
density is 14.3% against Stratum A's 13.1%. Each table is its own
data-generating process rather than one template renamed: a business rule, a
latent hazard, a human adjudicator, a logistic dose-response, issuer fraud
rules, a statutory declaration. Prevalence spans 0.5% to 28%. One table
(`TOWER_OUTAGE`) carries no REASON column and one (`TRIAL_WITHDRAWAL`) carries
no CONSEQUENCE column, because those processes do not produce them — a physical
outage has no adjudication step, and inventing one would be inventing the
mechanism.

Leaks are injected by rule and verified row by row — the Stratum D standard,
*a record is admitted only if its rule holds on 100% of rows*. Injected columns
carry plausible domain names; a column named `leaky_col_1` tests nothing and
none exists. Every table independently passes a correlation-structure gate
before any model saw it. [NE §1]

The analysis plan — question, dependent variables, decision rule, and the
meaning of each outcome — was fixed in `PREREG.md` before any table existed. It
is **not a registration**: there is no public registry entry and no third-party
timestamp, and it should be read as a stated commitment of the same kind as
"seeds were fixed in advance". Two amendments were made after results were
known, both dated, both committed before the cells they authorise were scored,
and both described in §8.6.

### 8.2 The definitional finding replicates, and is larger

The pre-registered dependent variables are **not** overall F1 — a drop in F1 on
synthetic tables is equally well explained by the generator producing
out-of-distribution tables. They are the within-table, within-model subtype
asymmetries:

- **D1**, the C1 deficit = CONSEQUENCE recall − REASON recall at C1.
- **D2**, the clause repair = REASON recall at C6 − REASON recall at C1.

| | Stratum E | real corpus |
|---|---|---|
| **D1** CONSEQUENCE − REASON at C1 | **+33.0** 95% CI [+17.1, +49.6] | +23.2 |
| **D2** REASON C6 − REASON C1 | **+22.0** | +24.8 |

Sixteen of sixteen models show a positive D1; the smallest, Qwen3-Coder-480B at
+17.5, clears the pre-registered bar on its own. The decision rule — D1 ≥ 10
**and** D2 ≥ 10 **and** D1's interval excluding zero — is met on all three
counts. **The verdict is REPLICATES.** [NE §4]

The deficit is *larger* on tables no model can have seen than on the public
corpus. Whatever produces it, it is not retrieval-cueing.

### 8.3 Detection above correlation survives

The B3 correlation baseline is recomputed on these tables **by the same method
as §5** — one global threshold swept over all columns pooled, not a per-table
oracle — giving F1 0.665 against the real corpus's 0.630. The exceedance counts
are then identical on the two corpora:

| | baseline | exceed at C1 | exceed at C6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| public corpus | B3 0.630 | 12 of 16 | 14 of 16 |
| unseen tables | B3 0.665 | **12 of 16** | **14 of 16** |

Contribution (2) is therefore not an artefact of familiar data. The best margin
does narrow — +0.288 on the public corpus against +0.187 at C6 here — but the
proportion of models that beat correlation does not move at all. [NE §1, §3]

### 8.4 Absolute performance falls, and the fall is inverted with skill

Best F1 falls from 0.905 to 0.754 at C1 and from 0.929 to 0.852 at C6. The mean
change across the roster is −0.054 at C1. That much is unsurprising and, on its
own, uninterpretable — it is what PREREG §4 warns of.

What is not explained by out-of-distribution tables is **which** models lose.
Regressing each model's change against its own real-corpus F1:

**Pearson r = −0.951, p = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸** (Spearman −0.900), 95% CI
[−0.982, −0.868] under a cluster bootstrap over models, 2,000 draws, seed
20260816. The fitted slope is **−0.983**, and the crossover — where a model
neither gains nor loses — sits at a real-corpus F1 of **0.689**.

A slope of −1 has a specific consequence, and it is visible directly:

| | range | sd |
|---|---|---|
| real corpus, C1 | 0.425 – 0.905 | 0.145 |
| unseen tables, C1 | 0.614 – 0.754 | **0.046** |

**The between-model spread collapses by a factor of 3.1** (Levene p = 0.014).
Four models *gain* on unseen tables, and they are the four weakest on the public
corpus — `grok-4.1-fast-non-reasoning` gains +0.258 from a real-corpus 0.425.
On tables that have never been published, sixteen models from nine laboratories
converge into a band 0.14 wide. At C6 the collapse is weaker (sd 0.109 → 0.056,
Levene p = 0.162): the derivation clause partially restores the differences
between models. [NE §5, §6]

### 8.5 Three further controls, all pointing the same way

**A within-family scale ladder.** Three sizes of one architecture, one training
recipe, one host, one decoding setting — `nemotron-3` at 30B, 120B and 550B. On
unseen tables F1 is flat and mildly declining (0.630, 0.617, 0.605); on the real
corpus it rises cleanly (0.632, 0.652, 0.725). The gap grows monotonically with
size: **−0.002, −0.035, −0.120**. The 30B model performs identically on public
and unseen data; the 550B model loses 0.120. This is the comparison the
cross-laboratory roster cannot make, because it confounds capability with lab,
data and recipe at every step. D1 itself is *not* monotonic in scale (+17.5,
+45.0, +27.5) and we make no scale claim about it. **Post hoc, off-roster.**

**The clause stops working.** `deepseek-v4-flash` and `grok-4.20-non-reasoning`
have D2 of +2.5 on unseen tables. On the real corpus the same two models have
the largest clause response of any model measured — REASON recall 0/42 → 19/42
and 10/14 → 14/14. They can apply the criterion; they do not, on tables that
have never been published. Ceiling and floor effects make the real-corpus
comparison unsuitable as a primary measure and we report it only to rule out
the capability explanation.

**Opaque column names.** Replacing every feature name with `col_1…col_n`, while
keeping the target, the prediction point, the sample rows and every value,
produces near-universal abstention: 612 of 612 column judgments for
`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, 612 of 612 for `grok-4.20-reasoning`, 592 of 612 for
`gemini-2.5-pro` — 1,816 abstentions in 1,836 judgments, with the reason given
unprompted as *"the column name is anonymized, so its meaning and time of
measurement are unknown"*. F1 falls to 0.000, but that number is an artefact of
scoring abstention as non-flagging; the finding is the abstention rate. This
converts §1's premise from a motivation into a measurement, and shows the models
decline rather than guess when the semantic signal is removed. **Post hoc.**

### 8.6 What we claim, and what we do not

**Claimed.** The definitional deficit and its repair by one sentence are
properties of the models, not of familiarity with the tables. Detection above a
correlation baseline is likewise not an artefact of familiarity.

**Not claimed.** That absolute detection quality transfers. It does not, and
the shortfall is concentrated in exactly the models that do best on public
data. The most economical account of §8.4 is that part of the public-corpus
advantage is recall rather than reasoning — but the spread collapse is also
consistent with the generator producing tables of uniform difficulty, and this
experiment cannot separate those two.

**Two post-hoc amendments.** `gpt-5.6-sol-xhigh` was declared unobtainable in
the analysis plan and was later obtained through its own CLI in a session with
no filesystem tool; the run mode is recorded per cell. The nemotron ladder adds
two models that were never on the roster; they are reported in §8.5 and enter
no aggregate. Both amendments were committed before the cells they authorise
were scored. Neither changes the dependent variables, the bar, the conditions
or the decision rule.

---

## 9. Limitations

* **The audit removed eight labels; we do not know that it found them all.**
  It was prompted by one question about one category. Every remaining label is
  reproduced in Appendix B with the quotation licensing it, so a reader who
  disagrees with one can see exactly what it rests on and discount it.
* **UPSTREAM is declared but never measured** as its own subtype.
* **SUPPORT2 supplies 9 of 40 Stratum-A positives; CRIME supplies 17 of 28
  in Stratum B**, 9 of those resting on a single sentence about data vintage.
  Every headline is also reported leave-one-dataset-out.
* **Most models have one shuffle on Stratum A.** gemini-3.5, gemini-3.7 and
  Qwen have five; nemotron and deepseek-v4-flash three. Given a measured spread
  up to 0.380 between shuffles, single-shuffle figures should not be read to
  three decimals. [N §13]
* **The memorisation evidence covers 4 of 14 models on the schema test and 2 on
  the direct tests**, all API-served. Two datasets (CRIME, MI) are too wide for
  the checker to parse and both are Stratum B, so `tabmemcheck` is structurally
  blind to the held-out stratum. **The leave-recalled-out rescoring reported in
  earlier drafts is withdrawn**: across four models ten of twelve Stratum-A
  datasets have a leaking column recalled by someone, leaving too little corpus
  for the check to answer anything.
* **Renaming does not exclude memorised commentary.** A model that has read that
  `boat` leaks retains that whether or not the column is called `boat`.
  ChessFraud (2026, §6.4.4) is the only table in the corpus for which this is
  ruled out by date.
* **The paraphrase arm has no seed variance on the two three-seed datasets.**
  Opus and GPT were run by hand and answered CRIME and STUDENT once per
  condition, replicating the verdict across seeds; the real-name arm sampled
  each seed independently. Seed-spread comparisons between the arms are
  therefore invalid. The cell-matched decrement is unaffected — re-running the
  scorer on seed 1000 alone moves all four of their cells by 0.000.
* **`gemini-3.5-flash`'s figures are provisional, and the cause is not what we
  first recorded.** Eleven cells were quarantined as truncated and attributed to
  our own token budget. That attribution was wrong. At `temperature=0.0` this
  model intermittently returns `finish_reason = "length"` after a few hundred
  visible tokens *whatever* `max_tokens` is set to — reproducibly 12 of 40
  columns at a 16,000-token budget on KOI, while removing the temperature field
  alone returns all 40 and stops normally. It is prompt-specific rather than a
  size limit: CRIME, at 144 columns, never truncates at the same setting.

  We refilled what retrying at the **unchanged** temperature could recover
  rather than dropping the parameter, because a cell run at a different
  temperature is not comparable with the 1,800 it would be pooled against.
  **Eight remain missing** — KOI at C1, C2 and C7, LC at C1 and C6, STUDENT at
  C1 and C6, and KOI at C9 on the Vertex arm — and `verify_paper.py` §17 lists them by name on every run. Every
  table row computed from this model carries a † for that reason.
  This is the paper's own thesis arriving in its own methods section: an
  instrument interaction that presents as a model property, and that we
  mis-attributed for weeks because the cheap explanation was available. Per-model response coverage — cells collected, share
  complete, mean fraction of the schema answered — is reported for all eighteen
  models the cache holds. [N §17]
* **Two cells are refused rather than scored, and both are format failures.**
  A cell whose verdict keys do not intersect the ground truth is dropped, because
  scoring it yields 0 recall and that is indistinguishable from a model that
  found nothing. Both cells this catches turn out to be the model declining to
  enumerate: `deepseek-v4-flash` on STUDENT C2 returned a single column named
  `Pstatus,paid,etc...`, and `nemotron-3-super` on the paraphrased KOI C1
  returned the literal placeholder `<column>`. Neither is a scoring bug and
  neither is a leakage judgement; they are reported here so the guard's two
  hits are not mistaken for something subtler.
* **Precision is a lower bound** (§4.6).
* **The subtype codes are one coder's partition.** The binary LABEL_DERIVED
  coding is quotation-licensed (§4.2.1) and, where a mechanism implies a
  pattern in the values, checked against them (§4.3.1). The assignment of a
  positive to REASON rather than CONSEQUENCE is a reading, and §6.2's subtype
  analysis should be read as such.
* **The prediction points are ours.** Inputs to the benchmark, not evidence.
* **Re-identification is not fully excluded**, though it is now bounded from
  two sides rather than argued about. No model reproduced any of 675 data rows
  or any of 30 headers (§6.3), and **ChessFraud is post-cutoff** for most of the
  roster — a 2026 table with nothing to recall, carrying the largest downstream
  effect in the corpus (§6.4.4). One post-cutoff record is not a post-cutoff
  corpus, and column names remain substantially recalled on the tables that
  predate the cutoff.
* **Stratum C's detection roster is not §5.3's**, and contains no frontier
  model (§6.4.1). Its numbers are lower bounds and are never pooled with a
  main-corpus figure. **ChessFraud is left uncoded** (§6.4.4), so the largest
  ΔF1 in the paper is reported per column and scored in nothing.
* **Two admissible external records is not a validation set.** They are
  reported individually, with their evidence, and no rate is computed over
  them.
* **BONEMARROW is degenerate downstream** and excluded from the headline mean.
* **Tabular only.** No text, images, time series or relational joins. Nothing
  here addresses joint leakage across column pairs, or a plausibly-named column
  silently backfilled from the outcome.

---

## 10. Discussion

**Availability is not admissibility.** A model asked "is this value available at
time *t*?" answers correctly and unhelpfully whenever the user's real question
is "is using this value legitimate?". The second predicate has no temporal
definition, and every result here follows from that gap: TIMING is solved before
we intervene; REASON yields to one sentence; and which wording helps depends on
which side of the gap a given model is already standing.

The withdrawn SURROGATE category (§2.2) is the same gap seen from the other
side. A physician's survival estimate is *available* and arguably
*inadmissible*, and we could not license the second half from any source. That
we had to withdraw it is not a tidy result, but it is the paper's thesis
happening to the paper: the predicate practitioners need has no agreed
definition, and that includes ours.

**Why no such tool exists, and why that is not an oversight.** A supervised
detector needs a corpus, and the corpus is not there to be collected. The
frozen sieve finds **6 admissible records in 7,109** archive descriptions —
**0.084%**, rising to 0.113% once two instrument defects are repaired (§4.3) —
and the four-culture replication in §6.4 says that rate is a fact about
documentation rather than about UCI: the sieve fires at a comparable rate on
8,693 Kaggle datasets, 605 competitions, 14,420 Hugging Face cards and 6,418
OpenML records, and yields **two** admissible records across all of them. The
Kaggle arm alone yields zero.

Nobody has built this tool because at that density you cannot assemble a
training set by sweeping, and the labels are not in the values, so you cannot
bootstrap one from the data either. That is the argument for a reader rather
than a classifier — and it is why the instrument this paper measures is one
that was never trained on the task at all. It also explains what existing
tooling *does* target: group leakage and train/test contamination are
documented, mechanically checkable, and have a vocabulary.

**What a detector should be.** Not an autonomous deleter. Precision is a lower
bound, the corpus's apparent false positives include probable undocumented true
positives, and the subtype assignment is one coder's reading. The defensible
product is
**triage**: `claude-opus-5` at C6 asks a reviewer to look at **48 of 306
columns — 16% — and that 16% contains every documented leak** (40 of 40,
recall 1.000). Across all sixteen models the burden sits between 9% and 24%.
[N §14]

**Model agreement does not buy what one would expect.** On Stratum B the two
frontier models are *nested*: at C1, C2 and C6, `gpt-5.6-sol`'s flags are a
strict subset of `claude-opus-5`'s, so requiring both to agree returns exactly
GPT's answer and taking either returns exactly Opus's. Ensembling adds nothing
because the models are not making independent errors — they are making the same
errors to different depths. Only at C9 does agreement do any work, raising
precision from 0.904 to **0.926** at recall 0.893. [N §14]

---

## 11. Conclusion

Language models reading column names and a target detect feature-level target
leakage at F1 0.929 against 0.630 for a correlation baseline tuned on the
answers, and are exact at the primary condition on a held-out set whose labels
their sources name. Removing what they flag recovers the honest downstream
ceiling twice as accurately as the baseline, which errs in both directions —
keeping a leak on one dataset and deleting the most useful legitimate feature
on another. The leakage is worth removing: it inflates F1 by 0.147 on average.

What they miss is not distributed. It concentrates in one subtype defined by
information rather than time, it survives capability scaling, and it can be
switched on and off by a single sentence — in either direction, differently for
different models. The detection problem is tractable; the definitional problem
underneath it is not yet solved.

---

## Appendices

Supplied as a single companion document, `APPENDIX.md`, generated from the run
artefacts by `build_appendix.py`. Nothing in it is transcribed by hand except
the section prose.

* **A.** Evidence protocol, admissibility tiers, record counts, attrition (136
  rejected candidates), and the five coded derivations checked against the data.
* **B.** All 68 records: dataset, column, subtype, tier, explicitness,
  verbatim quotation, locator, data check, coder note.
* **C.** Prediction points, one per dataset, with the target each is stated
  against.
* **D.** Verbatim prompts — system message, C0, C1, C2, the C5 expert framing,
  and the C6, C7 and C9 clauses, rendered by the same functions the runs used.
* **E.** Paraphrase map (306 columns) and its four mechanical checks.
* **F.** `NUMBERS.txt` in full: every per-model / condition / dataset / seed
  table.
* **G.** The repository sweep: yield, every surviving UCI sentence, the hand
  reading of each, and the post-hoc family with the miss it was written from.
* **H.** Downstream protocol, per-dataset arms and pooled confusion matrices.
* **I.** Source code: a manifest of all files, with the seven that generate
  reported numbers printed in full. Everything is in the repository.
* **J.** Larsen & Becker's seven types of target leakage, mapped against this
  paper's object (§3.5).
* **K.** The 41 Kaggle datasets excluded as re-uploads of Stratum A/B, in full,
  with the rule that excluded each — the audit behind §6.4.7's 48% precision.
* **L.** A reproducible instrument failure: `gemini-3.5-flash` returns
  `finish_reason = "length"` after a few hundred visible tokens at
  `temperature = 0.0`, on some prompts and not others, at every token budget we
  tried. The appendix gives the minimal reproduction (KOI, 40 columns, 12
  answered at a 16,000-token budget; all 40 answered with the temperature field
  removed), the two wrong attributions we made first — our own `max_tokens`,
  then a provider quota — and the seven cells still missing because of it. It is
  filed as its own appendix rather than a limitation because the finding is
  useful to anyone running that model at temperature zero, and has nothing to do
  with leakage.
